title: EFFECTS OF INDOOR LIGHTING, GENDER, AND AGE ON MOOD AND COGNITIVE PERFORMANCE
research_question: To investigate the younger and older adult females' and males' mood reactions to indoor lighting and their ongoing cognitive performances in that type of physical environment.

participants.description: Swedish adults. Mean age of women: 23.3 years (younger) and 65.2 years (older). Mean age of men: 23.9 years (younger) and 65.5 years (older).
participants.recruitment: Younger adults recruited from local college and employment exchange; seniors from local pensioners' clubs.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Office-like room (3.9m x 3.8m x 2.5m) with false windows, controlled noise (35 dBA) and air temperature (21°C). Two lighting conditions: (a) warm white lighting (3000 K, reddish, Osram, 36 W, L 36/22, CRI 95) and (b) cool white lighting (4000 K, bluish, Osram, 36 W, L 36/32, CRI 95). Both at 500 lux illuminance.

measures.instrument: Positive Affect Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) - delta score (Mood Block 2 minus Mood Block 1)
Positive Affect Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) - delta score (Mood Block 2 minus Mood Block 1)
7-adjective questionnaire (glaring, dim, soft, bright, warm, intense, cool) on 5-point scale
Free recall task (3 word-lists of 16 words each, neutral, negative, or positive hedonic tone)
18 multiple choice questions about a 7-page text

findings.antecedent: Gender (younger females vs. younger males) in indoor lighting conditions
findings.mechanism: Younger females preserved positive mood better than younger males.
findings.quote: the younger females preserved (had the least decrease in) the positive mood better than the younger males did

findings.antecedent: Gender (older males vs. older females) in indoor lighting conditions
findings.mechanism: Older males preserved positive mood better than older females.
findings.quote: The older males, on the other hand, preserved the positive mood better than the older females did

findings.antecedent: Gender (females vs. males) in indoor lighting conditions
findings.mechanism: Females preserved negative mood better than males (smallest increase was .78 vs. 2.25).
findings.quote: females preserved the negative mood better than did males (smallest increase was .78 vs. 2.25)

findings.antecedent: Cool white lighting (4000 K) for older adults vs. younger adults
findings.mechanism: Older adults preserved negative mood better in cool white lighting than younger adults.
findings.quote: the older adults preserved (had the smallest increase in) the negative mood better in the cool white lighting than did the younger adults

findings.antecedent: Warm white lighting (3000 K) for younger adults vs. older adults
findings.mechanism: Younger adults preserved negative mood better in warm white lighting than older adults.
findings.quote: The opposite result, however, was true for the warm white lighting

findings.mechanism: Younger adults performed significantly better than older adults (18.2 vs. 6.1 out of 32).
findings.quote: The younger performed significantly better than the older adults (younger = 18.2 vs. older = 6.1 out of 32).

findings.mechanism: Younger females performed better than younger males.
findings.quote: The younger females were also shown to perform better than the younger males

findings.mechanism: Younger participants performed significantly better than older participants (10.2 vs. 6.5 out of 18.0).
findings.quote: the younger participants performed significantly better than the older (younger = 10.2 vs. older = 6.5 out of 18.0).

findings.mechanism: Younger adults performed significantly better than older adults (9.7 vs. 8.9 out of 18).
findings.quote: The younger adults performed significantly better than the older, F(1, 72) = 5.79, p < .05 (younger = 9.7 vs. older = 8.9 out of 18).

findings.mechanism: Younger participants performed significantly better than their older colleagues (6.5 vs. 4.6 out of 16).
findings.quote: the younger participants performed significantly better than their older colleagues, F(1,72)=52.08, p < .001 (younger= 6.5 vs. older = 4.6 out of 16).

findings.mechanism: Women performed significantly better than men (6 vs. 5).
findings.quote: Women performed significantly better (6 vs. 5) than men, F(1, 72) = 13.36, p < .001.

findings.consequent: Recall of positive words (vs. negative words)
findings.mechanism: Participants recalled significantly more positive than negative words, consistent with a mood congruence effect.
findings.quote: The participants recalled significantly (F(2, 144) = 6.01, p < .01) more positive than negative words, t(79) = 3.36, p < .001.

findings.mechanism: Younger adults assessed the room light as brighter than older participants (3.4 vs. 2.8 on a 1-5 scale), possibly due to age-determined visual impairments.
findings.quote: the younger adults assessed the room light as brighter than the did the older participants (3.4 vs. 2.8 on a scale ranging from 1 to 5).

findings.mechanism: Younger participants assessed the room light as cooler than older colleagues (2.8 vs. 2.1 on a 1-5 scale), possibly due to age-determined visual impairments.
findings.quote: the younger participants assessed the room light as cooler than their older colleagues did (2.8 vs. 2.1 on a scale ranging from 1 to 5).

mechanisms: Indoor lighting acts as an affective source, conveying different emotional meanings to different age groups and genders.
Age-related visual impairments influence the perception of room light (brightness, coolness).
Mood congruence effect: current mood influences the recall of mood-congruent information.
implementation_implications: The color parameters of office lighting are important for an occupant's individual, psychological lighting-demands, especially considering age and gender differences in mood reactions to lighting.
limitations: The study did not find direct effects of lighting on mood, only moderated effects (gender, age, or both).
The interpretation of gender differences in short-term recall (women performing better than men) is difficult as the word lists were not gender-related and no interaction with word list was found.

paper_metadata.title: Effects of Indoor Lighting, Gender, and Age on Mood and Cognitive Performance
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effects of Indoor Lighting, Gender, and Age on Mood and Cognitive Performance
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The impact of indoor lighting, gender, and age on mood and cognitive performance was examined in a between-subject experiment. It was hypothesized that indoor lighting is an affective source that may convey emotional meanings differentiated by gender, age, or both. A two-way interaction between type of lamp and age on negative mood showed that younger adults (about 23 years old) best preserved a negative mood in the “warm” (more reddish) white lighting while working with a battery of cognitive tasks for 90 minutes; for the older adults (about 65 years old), “cool” (more bluish) white lighting accounted for the identical effect. The younger females were shown to preserve the positive mood as well as the negative mood better than the younger males, and a main effect of age in all cognitive tasks revealed the superiority of younger to older adults in cognitive performance.
